title: Algebra II — Common Core High School Math — Question Sets
id_format: S<set>-<section>-Q<number>. Section codes: M = MAIN (the course's own standard), B1, B2, ... = BACKWARD branches (a Grade K-8 standard, or a course standard that is the MAIN standard of an earlier set), F1 = FORWARD 1 and F2 = FORWARD 2 (standards of later courses; standard_course names the course). id is unique within this collection; uid = "A2:" + id is unique across all collections. Forward branches name standards only, never question IDs of other collections. Set and branch numbers are fixed: they need not be consecutive, and an ID is never reused for a different skill (see revisions.json).

relations.main: the Algebra II skill the set is built around (strand: core, or advanced extension (+))
relations.backward: a prerequisite obstacle to check when a student misses MAIN questions: a Grade K-8, Algebra I or Geometry standard, or the MAIN standard of an earlier Algebra II set; branch.alignment is exact or supporting
relations.forward1: the next demand after MAIN; branch.progression is same-course deepening, cross-standard extension, or later-course extension, and branch.new_demand states what it adds
relations.forward2: a further demand; branch.builds_on says how it builds on FORWARD 1 (or why it is a separate extension of MAIN)
relations.nearest_related: true marks a forward branch that no standard directly continues; it uses the nearest related standard

grading_rules: Match each student response to its key record by the question ID printed on the question page (for example S40-F2-Q3). The page number is the same in the Question Collection and the Answer Key. IDs are unique within one grade's collection; across collections use uid (for example G5:S40-F2-Q3).
Multiple choice and true/false: the response is correct when the chosen letter equals correct_letter, or when the student wrote the text of the correct choice.

Short answer: accept any mathematically equivalent form unless the question asks for a specific form (equivalent fractions, decimals, and mixed numbers; a ratio written as a : b, a to b, or a/b; "x = 5" or "5"; terms of an expression in any order). Units are not required unless the question asks for them.
When an answer has several parts (separated by semicolons, or with labels such as "Rate of change:"), every part must be correct.
Drawing / plotting questions (type plot): correct_answer describes what a correct drawing shows. Judge the student's drawing against it.

Drawing + written questions (type plot_text): the student draws on the figure AND writes an answer. drawing_answer describes the correct drawing and correct_answer the written answer. Both must be correct: every requested point, segment or shape in the drawing, and the written conclusion.

Answer with required work (type work): required_method says what the shown work must use. A correct final answer without that work earns partial credit only; correct work with a slip in the final answer is also partial.
Explain / describe questions: grading_note says what a correct response must include; accept any reasonable wording.
grading_note also lists other accepted answers and the work behind an answer. It is guidance for the grader, not for students.

Algebra II answer forms: the grading_note of every written answer begins with "Form required:" or with "Any" (for example "Any equivalent form"), which says what else is accepted. "Exact" means an exact value (fractions, radicals, logarithms, π, i); a decimal approximation alone is not full credit. When rounding is allowed the note names the precision; an answer within half a unit of the last required place is correct.

Solutions: a question says whether solutions are real or may be complex. A solution set must contain every solution (with multiplicity when the question asks for it); an extraneous value listed as a solution is an error. "No real solution" is an answer when the key says so. Complex numbers are written a + bi with real a and b unless a form is named.

Domains: logarithms are real only for positive arguments and bases b > 0, b ≠ 1; √(x²) = |x| over the reals; a rational expression keeps the exclusions of its original denominator after cancelling. Trigonometric questions state degrees or radians and an interval, and "all solutions" means every solution in that interval.

Proofs, derivations and explanations are multiple choice (no question needs a person to grade): the keyed choice is a complete, valid argument; each other choice is a flawed one (checking a few values, an invalid algebra step, assuming the result, a false fact, or the wrong direction or reflection), and grading_note says what is wrong with each.

Graphs are multiple choice (no question needs a drawing surface): the figure shows four candidate graphs labeled A to D on the same window, with asymptotes and midlines dashed and holes as open circles, and the choices are "Graph A" to "Graph D". grading_note lists the features of the correct graph and what each other graph shows.

Technology: a question that needs a calculator says so and names the capability (logarithms, normal cumulative probability, trigonometric values in radians or degrees). Simulation questions supply the simulated results; any answer that reads them correctly within the stated tolerance is accepted.
Every question has an explanation in its grading_note after the form rule; for numeric questions it shows the verified exact value and the work.
markup: prompt is plain text. prompt_markup uses {a/b} for a stacked fraction and 2{1/2} for a mixed number.
